questions.title: What Does the PM Say?
questions.storyContext: Before Parliament sees the brief, the PM wants your advice. He addresses the nation at 8am. Six million people remember the night the lights went out. They want to know: will it happen again? "What should I tell them?"
questions.facilitatorPrompt: Six million people hear whatever he says — and the full truth eventually comes out. Reassure and risk a leak, or tell all and risk fear?

options.label: Say the threat was handled quickly and systems worked as designed. Details about 12 substations risk panic.
options.consequence: Calm holds for nine days. Then a foreign newspaper prints "12 SUBSTATIONS" and the questions get much louder.

options.label: Tell everything: Singapore was attacked, 12 substations fell, it lasted hours — and here's exactly how we won.
options.consequence: The speech trends worldwide: scary, honest, calm. Polls wobble for a week — then trust climbs past pre-blackout levels.

options.label: Acknowledge a serious cyber incident — detected, contained, under review — without details that help the next attacker.
options.consequence: The 8am address lands steady and sober. Most people nod and go to work. The rumour mill hums — quietly.

options.label: Skip the attack details. Announce the $500M cybersecurity plan and talk about what comes next. Give them a plan, not a post-mortem.
options.consequence: The $500M headline drowns out the blackout for a news cycle. In Parliament, someone still asks: "But what happened?"

questions.title: What Do We Build?
questions.storyContext: Parliament approves $500M in emergency funding. You watched the readings climb, fought the intruder, relit 200,000 homes, built the case. Now the strategic call: what does Singapore build so nobody has to do what your team just did?
questions.facilitatorPrompt: Ten years of national strategy. What was the blackout's real lesson — fragile systems, slow recovery, or fighting alone?

options.label: Lock everything down. Trust nothing by default. Disconnect the most sensitive systems from the internet forever. Close every gap.
options.consequence: Singapore becomes the region's hardest target — and its slowest shipper. Attackers move to easier prey. Mostly.

options.label: Assume attacks will happen. Spread critical functions, self-repairing networks, AI handling the first wave. Make the next blackout last minutes, not hours.
options.consequence: Three years later, an attacker breaches a water plant — and the system reroutes around them in 40 seconds. They leave confused.

options.label: Singapore can't defend alone. Build a Southeast Asian cyber defence alliance — shared intel, joint response teams, collective defence.
options.consequence: Two years in, a partner state flags malware aimed at your port — days early. The shield is bigger than the island now.

options.label: Invest in people. Cyber hygiene for every citizen, security audits for every business, a national cyber reserve corps.
options.consequence: Five years on, a retiree reports a [[phishing]] email that turns out to be the opening move of a campaign. The reserve corps traces it.
